report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p = .11", "p = .66", "p > .25"), Sentence = c("Behavioural restraint did not change (d = -0.07, p = .11).", "Social media and web-use data did not change (d = 0.02, p = .66). info.title: Do people who care about their data and privacy know their data rights? Evidence from Estonia, 2023-2025

									Estonia

Estonian Institute for Health Development
								
									Estonia

text.text: European data protection law gives people rights over their personal data, but what motivates us to exercise those rights?
In three surveys of Estonian adults (2023-2025), we examined whether people who care about privacy also know their data protection rights.

Respondents valued privacy far more than they felt they had it and regarded all seven types of personal data asked about as sensitive; valuing privacy, attention to privacy, experienced privacy and security, and perceived data sensitivity rose slightly over the period.
Knowledge of data rights, by contrast, was low, did not rise, and was unrelated to privacy and data sensitivity.
The same five combinations of sensitivity and knowledge recurred in all three waves, and sociodemographic characteristics explained little of them.

Caring about personal data and privacy were thus unrelated to knowing one's rights, so efforts should be made to explain and bridge the gap between privacy/data concerns and the individual opportunities to mitigate them.

The large-scale collection and use of personal data shifts power towards those who collect it (van Dijck, 2014; Zuboff, 2019): they set the rules for how data is accessed and analysed, while privacy protection tends to treat individuals at best as passive data subjects (Mällo et al., 2026).
text.formatted: The large-scale collection and use of personal data shifts power towards those who collect it <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(van Dijck, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Zuboff, 2019)</ref>: they set the rules for how data is accessed and analysed, while privacy protection tends to treat individuals at best as passive data subjects <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Mällo et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: People increasingly take part in this arrangement under compulsion rather than by choice: providing personal data has become a condition for using schools, health care, banks and public services (Barassi, 2019).
text.formatted: People increasingly take part in this arrangement under compulsion rather than by choice: providing personal data has become a condition for using schools, health care, banks and public services <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Barassi, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: As these services move online, the law that protects citizens becomes invisible to them, and those who cannot see it are less able to use their rights on equal terms (Ranchordás, 2024).
text.formatted: As these services move online, the law that protects citizens becomes invisible to them, and those who cannot see it are less able to use their rights on equal terms <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Ranchordás, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: European data protection law responds largely by giving individuals rights: to access their data, to correct and delete it, to restrict and object to its processing, and not to be subject to decisions based solely on automated processing (Regulation (EU) 2016/679, Articles 15-22).

This places much of the work of protection on individuals. Solove (2013) argues that such self-management, though necessary, is asked to do more than it can: people cannot weigh every data relationship, and many harms arise only when data is combined.
text.formatted: This places much of the work of protection on individuals. <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Solove (2013)</ref> argues that such self-management, though necessary, is asked to do more than it can: people cannot weigh every data relationship, and many harms arise only when data is combined.

text.text: Yet as more decisions about people are based on data, their ability to see, understand and contest its use becomes increasingly important (Lehtiniemi and Haapoja, 2020), and the regulation itself aims to give people control of their own data (Regulation (EU) 2016/679, Recital 7).
text.formatted: Yet as more decisions about people are based on data, their ability to see, understand and contest its use becomes increasingly important <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Lehtiniemi and Haapoja, 2020)</ref>, and the regulation itself aims to give people control of their own data (Regulation (EU) 2016/679, Recital 7).

text.text: Rights that people do not know about, however, cannot be used (Potter et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Rights that people do not know about, however, cannot be used <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Potter et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The rights-based model therefore depends partly on people knowing their rights.
We ask whether this knowledge grows over time and whether people who care about privacy are more likely to have it.
We examine these questions in three surveys of Estonian adults conducted between 2023 and 2025.
Using your rights requires a reason to act and the means to act or, in terms of protection motivation theory, a threat appraisal and a coping appraisal (Rogers, 1975).
text.formatted: Using your rights requires a reason to act and the means to act or, in terms of protection motivation theory, a threat appraisal and a coping appraisal <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Rogers, 1975)</ref>.

text.text: In privacy research the first is conceptualized as privacy concern and the second as online privacy literacy, which includes knowledge of privacy rights and law as well as of protective strategies (Prince et al., 2023).
text.formatted: In privacy research the first is conceptualized as privacy concern and the second as online privacy literacy, which includes knowledge of privacy rights and law as well as of protective strategies <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Prince et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: More concerned people have been found to have greater privacy literacy (Prince et al., 2023; Weinberger et al., 2017) and to know more about privacy law (Hoofnagle and Urban, 2014).
text.formatted: More concerned people have been found to have greater privacy literacy <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Prince et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Weinberger et al., 2017)</ref> and to know more about privacy law <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Hoofnagle and Urban, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: These studies, however, measured privacy literacy broadly.
Knowledge also need not bring control: GDPR awareness has been negatively associated with perceived control over personal data (Prince et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Knowledge also need not bring control: GDPR awareness has been negatively associated with perceived control over personal data <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Prince et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Concern may also be general rather than informed: people tend to see abstract privacy risks as likely but know little about the specific harms that collected data can cause (Gerber et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Concern may also be general rather than informed: people tend to see abstract privacy risks as likely but know little about the specific harms that collected data can cause <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Gerber et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Studies of digital resignation, privacy apathy and privacy cynicism describe people who are concerned about the collection of their data but feel unable to act (Draper and Turow, 2019; Hargittai and Marwick, 2016; Hoffmann et al., 2016), including towards the state, whose digital services are hard to opt out of (Bagger et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Studies of digital resignation, privacy apathy and privacy cynicism describe people who are concerned about the collection of their data but feel unable to act <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Draper and Turow, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Hargittai and Marwick, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Hoffmann et al., 2016)</ref>, including towards the state, whose digital services are hard to opt out of <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Bagger et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: When a threat is perceived but the means to act are not, people tend to respond defensively, for example by avoiding the issue (Witte, 1992).
text.formatted: When a threat is perceived but the means to act are not, people tend to respond defensively, for example by avoiding the issue <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Witte, 1992)</ref>.

text.text: The digital resignation literature also suggests that people may value privacy without experiencing it.

This attitude-experience gap concerns whether people feel that their privacy is respected in the environments they use, and differs from the privacy paradox, a gap between attitudes and behaviour (Barth and de Jong, 2017).
text.formatted: This attitude-experience gap concerns whether people feel that their privacy is respected in the environments they use, and differs from the privacy paradox, a gap between attitudes and behaviour <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Barth and de Jong, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: We study three constructs.
Privacy sensitivity is how much people value privacy and act on it.
We measure it together with the experience of privacy, how secure and private people feel in digital environments, to capture the gap between the two.

Data sensitivity is how sensitive people consider different kinds of personal data; it is measured separately for each data type, because sensitivity varies by data type and context (Chen et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Data sensitivity is how sensitive people consider different kinds of personal data; it is measured separately for each data type, because sensitivity varies by data type and context <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Chen et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Rights knowledge is whether people know which data protection rights are in force, a basic layer of the capability to act on one's data that a survey can measure.
Below, caring refers to the two kinds of sensitivity and knowing to rights knowledge.
Because using rights requires both, what matters is how privacy and data sensitivity and rights knowledge combine within individuals.
Westin's typology of privacy fundamentalists, pragmatists and unconcerned uses attitudes alone and assumes that people know how their data is protected (Hoofnagle and Urban, 2014).
text.formatted: Westin's typology of privacy fundamentalists, pragmatists and unconcerned uses attitudes alone and assumes that people know how their data is protected <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Hoofnagle and Urban, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: When tested, most respondents misunderstood these protections, and Urban and Hoofnagle (2014) proposed separating a more knowledgeable "privacy resilient" group from a less knowledgeable "privacy vulnerable" one.
text.formatted: When tested, most respondents misunderstood these protections, and <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Urban and Hoofnagle (2014)</ref> proposed separating a more knowledgeable "privacy resilient" group from a less knowledgeable "privacy vulnerable" one.

text.text: European typologies have combined GDPR awareness with digital experience (Rughinis , et al., 2021) and the importance of privacy with GDPR knowledge (Hanneke et al., 2023), but each was estimated in a single survey only.
text.formatted: European typologies have combined GDPR awareness with digital experience <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Rughinis , et al., 2021)</ref> and the importance of privacy with GDPR knowledge <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Hanneke et al., 2023)</ref>, but each was estimated in a single survey only.

text.text: Previous research leaves four gaps.
First, repeated population-level measurement is limited.

Eurobarometer surveys have tracked GDPR awareness since 2019, but with changing wording and survey modes, and mostly ask whether people have heard of the regulation rather than which rights they know (European Commission, 2019a , 2024).

text.text: National studies of rights knowledge are usually single cross-sections (Sideri and Gritzalis, 2020; Strycharz et al., 2020); four Norwegian surveys over five years found little change after the GDPR took effect (Presthus and Sørum, 2024).

text.text: Second, the link between caring and knowing has rarely been tested for knowledge of rights.
Third, privacy typologies are rarely estimated in more than one sample.
Fourth, findings on who cares and who knows are partly mixed.

GDPR awareness is predicted by education, occupation and age but little by gender, and sociodemographic characteristics together explain only a modest share of it (Rughinis , et al., 2021; Sideri and Gritzalis, 2020).

text.text: Estonia is a useful test case: everyday contact with personal data is more routine there than in most countries.
Nearly all public services are available online (e-Estonia, n.d.), and more than nine in ten internet users interact with public authorities online (Eurostat, 2024).
text.formatted: Nearly all public services are available online (e-Estonia, n.d.), and more than nine in ten internet users interact with public authorities online <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Eurostat, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: An effectively mandatory digital identity (Tsap et al., 2017) and a common data exchange layer (Solvak et al., 2019) make contact with state-held personal data routine.
text.formatted: An effectively mandatory digital identity <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Tsap et al., 2017)</ref> and a common data exchange layer <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Solvak et al., 2019</ref>) make contact with state-held personal data routine.

text.text: Hence, if such contact builds knowledge of data rights, this should show in Estonia.

Use, however, often outpaces understanding: Estonians knew little about their rights regarding automated decision-making while being the most enthusiastic of three countries about automating public administration (Kaun et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Use, however, often outpaces understanding: Estonians knew little about their rights regarding automated decision-making while being the most enthusiastic of three countries about automating public administration <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Kaun et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In 2024, 29% of Estonians had heard of the GDPR and knew what it is, against 40% across the EU (European Commission, 2024), and their awareness of specific rights was close to the EU average, although they were more than twice as likely to report having exercised their right of access (39% vs 18%; European Commission, 2019a).

The Data Tracker, which shows which public institutions have accessed one's data in selected registries (Solvak and Lauringson, 2024), had by late 2023 been heard of by 41% of residents and used by 13%, fewer among non-Estonians (Ministry of Economic Affairs and Communications [MEAC], 2023).

text.text: In short, Estonians use digital services extensively but know relatively little about the rules that govern personal data.
To address these gaps, we formulated five research questions (RQ): RQ1.
How much do Estonians value privacy compared with how private and secure they feel online, how sensitive do they consider their personal data, and how well do they know their data protection rights?
RQ2.
Did privacy sensitivity, data sensitivity and rights knowledge change between 2023 and 2025?
RQ3.
Are privacy sensitivity and rights knowledge related: do those who care more about privacy know more about their rights?
RQ4.
What combinations of sensitivity and rights knowledge characterise the population, and do the same combinations recur across the three waves?
RQ5.
How are these measures and combinations associated with gender, age, ethnicity, education and income?

We conducted three online surveys of Estonian adults aged 18 and over: Wave 1 in June 2023 (n = 1,503), Wave 2 in October 2023 (n = 1,702) and Wave 3 in December 2025 (n = 1,005), all conducted by Saar Poll, an Estonian social and market research company, in the Norstat Estonia online panel, with quotas for gender, age group, ethnicity, education and county of residence (Appendix A2).
The questionnaire was available in Estonian and Russian.
In late summer 2023, a research project used Estonian population register data to contact childless women about the reasons for their childlessness, prompting wide public debate (Pärli, 2023).
text.formatted: In late summer 2023, a research project used Estonian population register data to contact childless women about the reasons for their childlessness, prompting wide public debate <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Pärli, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: We brought Wave 2 forward to October 2023 to study its possible effects.
All Wave 1 respondents were invited to Wave 2 and 947 took part; new respondents filled the quotas (Appendix A2).
Wave 3 was a new sample.
We treat the waves as cross-sections: change is tested only between the independent Waves 1 and 3, collected 30 months apart, and Wave 2 is used descriptively and in the latent class models.
Longitudinal analyses of Waves 1 and 2 and the effects of the incident are reported separately (Authors, in preparation).

text.text: Wave 3 had more respondents in the lower income group (42% vs 31% in Wave 1) and slightly fewer with higher education (32% vs 36%).
Its income question was also worded differently, with different bands (Appendix A1), so part of the income difference may be due to the question.
All comparisons between Waves 1 and 3 were therefore repeated with sociodemographic characteristics controlled.
People who rarely use the internet are not represented, but over 90% of Estonian adults aged 16-74 use it regularly (Eurostat, 2025).

text.text: All analyses are unweighted (Appendix A2).

Established multidimensional instruments of privacy concern (Malhotra et al., 2004; Smith et al., 1996) have not fully held up in independent validation (Groß, 2021), and as the surveys also covered other topics, we used a shorter set of items.

text.text: Privacy sensitivity was measured with five statements on a four-point agreement scale (1-4): privacy is important to me in general (PRIV1); I pay close attention to ensuring my privacy and security in digital environments (PRIV2); I have sometimes refrained from doing something online or on my phone because it leaves a trace (PRIV3); I feel secure in all kinds of digital environments (PRIV4); and I feel private in all kinds of digital environments (PRIV5).
PRIV1 to PRIV3 measure privacy sensitivity and PRIV4 and PRIV5 the experience of privacy.
Because their means differ by up to one scale point, they are analysed individually.
A sixth statement (Waves 1 and 2 only) is not analysed.

Data sensitivity was measured by asking respondents to compare seven types of personal data and rate how sensitive each is for them (1-4): financial, communication, health, family and contact details, basic identifiers (name, personal identification code and date of birth), location, and social media and web-use data.
The items formed a reliable scale in every wave (Cronbach's 𝛼 = .86, .84 and .79; McDonald's 𝜔 similar) and are analysed individually and as a mean composite.
Genetic data (Waves 1 and 2 only) is excluded.

Rights knowledge was measured by asking which of six GDPR rights respondents believed to be in force in Estonia: to access one's data, to restrict its processing, to receive a copy, to correct and delete it, to object to conclusions drawn from it, and not to be subject to decisions based solely on automated processing (Articles 15-18, 21 and 22).
All six are in force, so "in force" is the correct answer, and the knowledge score counts the rights identified as in force (0-6).
For the rights, "don't know" was kept as a separate answer, because uncertainty is part of what we measure; for the sensitivity items it was treated as missing.
The sociodemographic characteristics were gender, age, ethnicity (self-reported, Estonian or other), education and income.

Waves 1 and 2 also measured risk-taking propensity and general trust (single items, 0-10) and satisfaction with five life domains (four-point scale), analysed for Wave 1 to check whether the patterns reflect general dispositions rather than orientations towards privacy.
Comparisons and associations.
Means of the privacy items and data sensitivity were compared between Waves 1 and 3 with independent-samples t-tests (Cohen's d), and answers for each right with 𝜒 2 tests (df = 2; Cramér's V).

Because the samples differed in composition, each comparison was repeated in a linear model controlling for age (continuous), gender, ethnicity, education and income, with identifying a right as in force as the outcome for the rights measure (Appendix D1).
Relations among the constructs were estimated within each wave with Pearson correlations and 95% confidence intervals, using pairwise deletion (Appendix B6).
Privacy sensitivity was represented by importance (PRIV1) and behavioural restraint (PRIV3), its attitudinal and behavioural expressions.
Attention to privacy (PRIV2) and the experience items (PRIV4, PRIV5) were correlated with knowledge separately.

Associations with sociodemographic characteristics, and in Wave 1 with the psychological measures, were tested within Waves 1 and 3, one characteristic at a time, with t-tests, one-way ANOVAs (𝜂 2 ) and, for the rights, 𝜒 2 tests (Cramér's V).

Differences between waves in these associations were tested only for the two rights whose associations with gender and income differed most (wave × predictor interactions; Appendix D2); other such differences are not interpreted.
With samples of 1,000 to 1,700, small effects reach significance, so we interpret only effects of at least d = 0.20 or 𝜂2 = .01.
All tests use 𝛼 = .05 without correction for multiple comparisons.
Analyses were conducted in JASP 0.95.4 (JASP Team, 2025) and IBM SPSS Statistics, Version 31 (IBM Corp., 2026).
Latent class analysis.
Latent class analysis (LCA) identified groups with distinct combinations of sensitivity and rights knowledge.
Models were estimated separately for each wave with 18 categorical indicators: the five privacy items, the seven data types and the six rights (model specification in Appendix C0).

We used poLCA (Linzer and Lewis, 2011) in R (4.1; R Core Team, 2025), retaining respondents with incomplete answers, and checked fit indices with snowRMM (Seol, 2023) in jamovi (2.4; The jamovi project, 2025).
text.formatted: We used poLCA <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Linzer and Lewis, 2011)</ref> in R (4.1; R Core Team, 2025), retaining respondents with incomplete answers, and checked fit indices with snowRMM <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Seol, 2023)</ref> in jamovi (2.4; The jamovi project, 2025).

text.text: Models with one to seven classes were compared on AIC, BIC, sample-size-adjusted BIC, entropy, smallest class size, convergence, interpretability and reproducibility across waves (Appendix C1).
Some criteria kept improving beyond five classes in Waves 1 and 2, but the five-class solution was retained because its classes were distinct, interpretable and recurred in every wave.
Classes were matched across waves by their conditional response profiles; measurement invariance was not tested formally (Appendix C2).
Respondents were assigned to the class with the highest posterior probability (modal assignment), which ignores classification uncertainty, so results based on it are interpreted cautiously.

In each wave, class membership was regressed on the five sociodemographic characteristics in a multinomial logistic regression in JASP (likelihood-ratio tests, Nagelkerke R² ; Appendix C4), and associations with the psychological measures (Wave 1) were tested with Cramér's V.

We used Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic) and GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI) (by Author 1 and 2, respectively) in preparing this manuscript.
Statistical output from JASP (aggregate results only; no raw data were shared) was entered into the tool to extract estimates and arrange them into tables and figures.
The tool was also used to check the consistency of the Results and Discussion, to edit the text for language and brevity, and to format the references.
The authors conducted all analyses, checked all AI-assisted output against the original output and sources, and take full responsibility for the content.

We first describe results on privacy sensitivity, data sensitivity and rights knowledge (RQ1, RQ2), then how sensitivity and knowledge combine (RQ3, RQ4), and finally how they vary across sociodemographic groups (RQ5).
Comparisons over time are made between Waves 1 and 3.
In every wave, respondents valued privacy more than they experienced it in digital environments (Figure 1).

text.text: Importance of privacy (PRIV1) averaged 3.38 to 3.55, while feeling secure (PRIV4: 2.48 to 2.61) and feeling private (PRIV5: 2.33 to 2.50) were rated lowest, averaging close to the midpoint of the four-point scale (2.5), between 'rather disagree' and 'rather agree'.
Attention to privacy and behavioural restraint fell in between.

The gap between valuing and experiencing privacy, about one scale point (0.86 to 1.07), was larger than any change between waves (at most 0.28) and more than twice the largest difference between sociodemographic groups on any item (0.44; Appendix B2).  B1.

Behavioural restraint did not change (d = -0.07, p = .11).
All seven data types were rated as sensitive (Figure 2): every mean was above 3, and the types differed by at most half a scale point.

text.text: Financial, communication and health data were rated highest (3.35 to 3.58) and social media and web-use data lowest (3.06 and 3.08).
Health data moved from third place in Wave 1 to first in Wave 3 (3.58, ahead of financial and communication data at 3.54).
Between Wave 1 and Wave 3, the composite rose from 3.24 to 3.40 (d = 0.28), also with sociodemographics controlled (Appendices B3, D1).

Six of the seven data types increased in perceived sensitivity: most for health (d = 0.32), location (d = 0.30) and communication data (d = 0.23), and less for contact and family data (d = 0.20), financial data (d = 0.16) and basic identifiers (d = 0.14).
Social media and web-use data did not change (d = 0.02, p = .66).  B3.

text.text: Knowledge varied widely by right (Figure 3).
text.formatted: Knowledge varied widely by right (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3</ref>).

text.text: In Wave 1, most respondents knew the rights to access their data (62%), to restrict processing (59%) and to receive a copy (54%); fewer knew the rights to correct and delete their data (46%), to object to conclusions drawn from it (37%) and not to be subject to solely automated decisions (28%).
Respondents who did not identify a right as in force mostly answered "don't know" rather than "not in force" (Appendix B5.1).
On average, respondents identified fewer than three of the six rights (2.86 in Wave 1 and 2.65 in Wave 3).
Rights knowledge did not increase between Wave 1 and Wave 3.
Five rights did not change (Cramér's V ≤ .04; Appendix B5.1).
Knowledge of the right to restrict processing fell from 59% to 44% (𝜒 2 (2) = 55.13, p < .001, V = .15), also with sociodemographics controlled (Appendix D1).
text.formatted: Knowledge of the right to restrict processing fell from 59% to 44% (𝜒 2 (2) = 55.13, p < .001, V = .15), also with sociodemographics controlled (Appendix D1).

text.text: The lost share moved mainly to "don't know" (31% to 40%) and partly to "not in force" (10% to 16%).

Within each wave, importance of privacy (PRIV1), behavioural restraint as a privacy strategy (PRIV3) and data sensitivity were weakly to moderately related to one another (r = .20 to .37), but not to the number of rights identified (r = -.07 to .05; Appendix B6).
All confidence intervals lay within ±.13, making larger correlations unlikely, and only one correlation reached significance (importance in Wave 3, r = -.07, p = .03).
Attention to privacy (PRIV2), the item that rose most, was also unrelated to knowledge (r = -.05 to .04).
Feeling secure and feeling private, by contrast, were positively correlated with knowledge in every wave (r = .19 to .26 and .14 to .20, all p < .001).
text.formatted: Feeling secure and feeling private, by contrast, were positively correlated with knowledge in every wave (r = .19 to .26 and .14 to .20, all p < .001).

text.text: A five-class solution was retained in each wave (Appendix C1), with good classification quality (entropy = .88, .86 and .87) and no class below 9% of the sample.
The same five combinations recurred in all three waves (Appendix C2).

Three classes combined high data sensitivity with uncertain (CLASS-2), misinformed (CLASS-3) or accurate knowledge of rights (CLASS-4), and two combined moderate sensitivity with uncertain (CLASS-1) or accurate knowledge (CLASS-5); the privacy items differed less across the classes (see below).
The uncertain and misinformed classes identified similarly few rights, but CLASS-1 and CLASS-2 mostly answered "don't know" and CLASS-3 "not in force".
CLASS-1 in Wave 1 differed most from its later counterparts, with lower data sensitivity and more rights identified (Appendix C5), but it still matched CLASS-1 most closely.
Two measures separated the classes in every wave: class membership explained 56 to 64% of the variance in data sensitivity and 65 to 71% in rights knowledge, but only 4 to 18% in any privacy item.
CLASS-4 and CLASS-5 identified around four of the six rights and CLASS-1, CLASS-2 and CLASS-3 fewer than two.
On data sensitivity, CLASS-2, CLASS-3 and CLASS-4 averaged 3.2 to 3.8 (highly sensitive) and CLASS-1 and CLASS-5 2.1 to 2.9 (moderately sensitive).

The two divisions cut across each other (Figure 4): CLASS-2 and CLASS-4 rated data almost equally sensitive in Waves 2 and 3 (3.66 vs 3.69; 3.62 vs 3.72), yet differed by more than three and a half rights in every wave.

text.text: The privacy items differed in the same way in every wave: the three highly sensitive classes (CLASS-2 -CLASS-4) rated privacy as more important, paid more attention to it and more often refrained from online activities than CLASS-1 and CLASS-5, so privacy sensitivity followed the same division as data sensitivity.
Feeling secure and private was lowest in CLASS-3, second lowest in CLASS-2 and highest in CLASS-5 (Figure 4; Appendix C5).
text.formatted: Feeling secure and private was lowest in CLASS-3, second lowest in CLASS-2 and highest in CLASS-5 (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">4</ref>; Appendix C5).

text.text: Class shares differed by no more than five percentage points between waves, and CLASS-4 and CLASS-5 were the two largest classes throughout (together 56 to 58%).
Effect sizes are summarised in Appendices B2.0, B4.0 and B5.2, and full results are in Appendices B2.1-B2.5, B4.1-B4.8 and B5.3.
All associations were small.

The strongest explained about 6% of the variance (age and the sensitivity of basic identifiers in Wave 3, 𝜂2 = .06), the largest group difference was d = 0.45 (gender, basic identifiers), and the strongest association with any right was V = .23 (age, right to restrict processing).
Rights knowledge was associated with age and ethnicity for all six rights in both waves (V = .09 to .23): respondents under 45 and ethnic Estonians identified more rights.

Gender was weakly associated with all rights in Wave 1 (V = .07 to .09), mainly because women more often answered "don't know" and men "not in force", while the shares answering "in force" differed by at most five percentage points.
In Wave 3, women less often identified the rights to object to conclusions (32% vs 40%) and not to be subject to automated decisions (22% vs 28%), answering "don't know" instead (V = .16 and .18).
Women rated personal data as more sensitive than men (composite: d = 0.25 in Wave 1 and 0.30 in Wave 3; five of seven types in both waves) without identifying more rights.

On the privacy items, ethnic Estonians reported more behavioural restraint in Wave 1 and felt more secure in both waves, women rated privacy as more important than men, and the youngest (18-24) rated it least important.
Education was associated with almost nothing: 6 of 38 tests reached significance, all with negligible effects (𝜂2 ≤ .01, V ≤ .08).
In both waves, every subgroup rated the importance of privacy at least half a scale point above feeling secure or private (0.50 to 1.33 points; Appendix B2).
Sociodemographic characteristics explained little of class membership (Nagelkerke R² = .13, .16 and .18 in Waves 1 to 3).
Age, gender and ethnicity contributed in all waves (p < .001), income weakly (p = .01 to .04) and education only in Wave 2 (Appendix C4).
text.formatted: Age, gender and ethnicity contributed in all waves (p < .001), income weakly (p = .01 to .04) and education only in Wave 2 (Appendix C4).

text.text: In every wave (Appendix C3), CLASS-4 was the youngest class (roughly a third under 35) and CLASS-1 and CLASS-2 the oldest (30 to 39% aged 65 or over); the classes with accurate knowledge, CLASS-4 and CLASS-5, had fewer respondents of other ethnicities (19 to 29%) than the other three (32 to 51%); and women were overrepresented in CLASS-2 and CLASS-4.
The psychological measures (Wave 1) were associated mainly with feeling secure and private (𝜂2 ≤ .03) and only weakly with class membership (Cramér's V = .06 to .10).
None of the four wave × predictor interactions tested for two rights was significant (all p > .25; Appendix D2).
text.formatted: None of the four wave × predictor interactions tested for two rights was significant (all p > .25; Appendix D2).

text.text: Respondents cared about privacy and their personal data, but those who were more sensitive did not know their rights any better, and high data sensitivity occurred both with and without knowledge of rights (CLASS-2 and CLASS-4).
Because the sensitivity measures were related to one another but not to knowledge, this is unlikely to reflect weak measures.
The concern was also general rather than informed: respondents rated all seven data types as sensitive, within half a scale point, and their ratings formed a single scale.
People may thus regard their data as sensitive without knowing what each kind of data can reveal (Gerber et al., 2019) or what they can do about it.
text.formatted: People may thus regard their data as sensitive without knowing what each kind of data can reveal <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Gerber et al., 2019)</ref> or what they can do about it.

text.text: In terms of protection motivation theory (Rogers, 1975), respondents had a reason to act but often lacked the means, a situation in which people tend to respond defensively (Witte, 1992).
text.formatted: In terms of protection motivation theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Rogers, 1975)</ref>, respondents had a reason to act but often lacked the means, a situation in which people tend to respond defensively <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Witte, 1992)</ref>.

text.text: Two results, discussed below, fit this reading, (although we did not measure efficacy beliefs or fear directly): those who knew fewer rights felt less secure and private, and between 2023 and 2025, privacy and data sensitivity rose while rights knowledge and behavioural restraint did not.
The decoupling also appeared at group level: the groups that knew more were not the groups that cared more.
Respondents under 45 identified more rights, yet the youngest (18-24) rated privacy as least important; women rated personal data as more sensitive than men but did not identify more rights.
This differs from earlier studies, in which people more concerned about privacy also knew more about it (Hoofnagle and Urban, 2014; Prince et al., 2023; Weinberger et al., 2017).
text.formatted: This differs from earlier studies, in which people more concerned about privacy also knew more about it <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Hoofnagle and Urban, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Prince et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Weinberger et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Those studies measured knowledge broadly, as online privacy literacy or knowledge of privacy law and business practices; for knowledge of one's own data protection rights, we found no such link.

Five and seven and a half years after the GDPR came to full effect (Waves 1 and 3, respectively), respondents identified fewer than three of the six data rights on average, with no rise between 2023 and 2025, as in Norway (Presthus and Sørum, 2024).
text.formatted: Five and seven and a half years after the GDPR came to full effect (Waves 1 and 3, respectively), respondents identified fewer than three of the six data rights on average, with no rise between 2023 and 2025, as in Norway <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Presthus and Sørum, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Because all rights were in force and presented for recognition, our measure is more likely to overstate than understate knowledge; recalling a right unprompted, or knowing how to use it, is harder.

As in other European surveys, the right not to be subject to solely automated decisions was the least known (European Commission, 2019a; Rughinis , et al., 2021; Strycharz et al., 2020), matching Estonians' limited knowledge of these rights despite their enthusiasm for e.g. automated public administration (Kaun et al., 2024a).
text.formatted: As in other European surveys, the right not to be subject to solely automated decisions was the least known <ref type="bibr">(European Commission, 2019a;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Rughinis , et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Strycharz et al., 2020)</ref>, matching Estonians' limited knowledge of these rights despite their enthusiasm for e.g. automated public administration <ref type="bibr">(Kaun et al., 2024a)</ref>.

text.text: This matters because automated decisions are becoming more common, including in public administration.
Only knowledge of the right to restrict processing changed, and it fell between Wave 1 and Wave 3.

This may reflect growing acceptance of routine processing as a norm that cannot be contested, which this right most directly challenges, and would fit the resignation discussed below; but as only one item changed and the order of question blocks differed in Wave 3, this interpretation remains tentative.
Knowledge of rights was also unequal across sociodemographic groups.
Younger respondents and ethnic Estonians knew more rights.
As non-Estonians are also less aware of the Estonian Data Tracker (MEAC, 2023), information about data rights may reach them less well.

Because the rights-based model protects those who know how to claim their rights, rights that formally apply to everyone are in practice less available to older and non-Estonian residents (Ranchordás, 2024).
text.formatted: Because the rights-based model protects those who know how to claim their rights, rights that formally apply to everyone are in practice less available to older and non-Estonian residents <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Ranchordás, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Education hardly mattered, although it predicts GDPR awareness in Europe (Rughinis , et al., 2021) and Data Tracker awareness in Estonia (MEAC, 2023), perhaps because we asked about specific rights rather than familiarity with a regulation or service.

text.text: We expected routine contact with personal data in Estonia to be reflected in better knowledge of rights, but this was not the case.

Estonians were more than twice as likely as the EU average to report having exercised their right of access, yet no more aware of specific rights (European Commission, 2019a), perhaps counting routine viewing of their records in e-services as an instance of using that right.

Such general self-reports probably overstate formal use of the right: when Dutch respondents were asked about specific actions rather than about rights in general, only 3% had formally requested access to their data (Strycharz et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Such general self-reports probably overstate formal use of the right: when Dutch respondents were asked about specific actions rather than about rights in general, only 3% had formally requested access to their data <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Strycharz et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Even people who obtain their data through formal requests often struggle to make sense of it (Bowyer et al., 2022). eeing one's data does not by itself seem to build knowledge of rights.

text.text: It may help if services present access to one's data explicitly as the use of a right, and of course, if people regard data as theirs.
Respondents valued privacy about one scale point more than they felt secure or private in digital environments, in every wave and group.
Part of this may reflect wording, as the experience items refer to all kinds of digital environments.
However, a gap of at least half a scale point in every group is unlikely to be a wording effect alone.

This gap concerns experience rather than behaviour and is in line with findings on digital resignation and privacy cynicism (Draper and Turow, 2019; Hargittai and Marwick, 2016; Hoffmann et al., 2016).
text.formatted: This gap concerns experience rather than behaviour and is in line with findings on digital resignation and privacy cynicism <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Draper and Turow, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Hargittai and Marwick, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Hoffmann et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Resignation may also arise towards the state, which is harder to opt out of than commercial services (Bagger et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Resignation may also arise towards the state, which is harder to opt out of than commercial services <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Bagger et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Estonians trust public institutions with their data more than companies (Puusalu and Marnot, 2021), but few check how the state uses it: by late 2023, 13% had used the Data Tracker (MEAC, 2023).
text.formatted: Estonians trust public institutions with their data more than companies <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Puusalu and Marnot, 2021)</ref>, but few check how the state uses it: by late 2023, 13% had used the Data Tracker (MEAC, 2023).

text.text: As our items did not distinguish public from commercial environments, whether the gap concerns either or both remains open.

Feeling secure and private, however, was related to knowledge of rights: classes with accurate knowledge felt more secure and private than classes with similar sensitivity but uncertain knowledge (CLASS-4 vs CLASS-2, CLASS-5 vs CLASS-1), and the misinformed CLASS-3 felt least so (Figure 4; Appendix C5).
text.formatted: Feeling secure and private, however, was related to knowledge of rights: classes with accurate knowledge felt more secure and private than classes with similar sensitivity but uncertain knowledge (CLASS-4 vs CLASS-2, CLASS-5 vs CLASS-1), and the misinformed CLASS-3 felt least so (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">4</ref>; Appendix C5).

text.text: In a Europe-wide survey, by contrast, GDPR awareness was associated with lower perceived control over personal data (Prince et al., 2024).
text.formatted: In a Europe-wide survey, by contrast, GDPR awareness was associated with lower perceived control over personal data <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Prince et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The findings need not conflict: learning how one's data is used can raise unease (Weinshel et al., 2019), while knowing what one can do about it may reduce it, as protection motivation theory would predict.
text.formatted: The findings need not conflict: learning how one's data is used can raise unease <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Weinshel et al., 2019)</ref>, while knowing what one can do about it may reduce it, as protection motivation theory would predict.

text.text: Part of this association may reflect ethnicity, although CLASS-3 felt least secure even in Wave 3, when its ethnic composition resembled that of the full sample.

The direction of the association is unknown: knowing one's rights may make people feel protected, or feeling unprotected may make them doubt that rights exist, as CLASS-3's "not in force" answers suggest.
Over time the two did not move together: between Waves 1 and 3, feeling private rose while rights knowledge did not, so the rise in feeling private cannot be attributed to better knowledge of rights.
Between 2023 and 2025, most measures of privacy and data sensitivity rose while knowledge of rights did not.
Attention to privacy rose most, but behavioural restraint, the only item about something respondents had actually done, did not change.

Among data types, the perceived sensitivity of health and location data rose most, and health data moved from third to first place, having ranked below financial and communication data in 2021 (Puusalu and Marnot, 2021) and in Wave 1.

text.text: Several data cases were widely reported in Estonia between Waves 1 and 3.
After the 2023 debate about the use of register data (see Methods), Wave 2 means, collected about seven weeks later, were close to those of Wave 1 (Figures 1 2 3).

text.text: Later, a breach exposed the identification numbers, contact details and purchase histories of about 700,000 pharmacy customers (ERR, 2024), and the Chancellor of Justice questioned the legal basis of police number-plate cameras that record vehicle movements (ERR, 2025).

text.text: Health and location data, which rose most, correspond to these two cases.
Our design cannot show causation (see Limitations), but during repeated public data cases, sensitivity rose without any gain in knowledge of rights.
Media coverage of such cases may make risks more visible, but it does not necessarily tell people what they can do.
The latent class structure, by contrast, did not change.
The same five classes recurred in three waves over two and a half years, with no class share changing by more than five percentage points, which addresses the gaps noted in the Introduction.
Whether individuals kept their class membership is examined in a a separate manuscript (Authors, in preparation).
text.formatted: Whether individuals kept their class membership is examined in a a separate manuscript <ref type="bibr">(Authors, in preparation)</ref>.

text.text: The classes extend earlier typologies.
CLASS-2, the largest class with poor knowledge, resembles the "privacy vulnerable" group of Urban and Hoofnagle (2014) but rates personal data as highly sensitive.
text.formatted: CLASS-2, the largest class with poor knowledge, resembles the "privacy vulnerable" group of <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Urban and Hoofnagle (2014)</ref> but rates personal data as highly sensitive.

text.text: Compared with earlier typologies, ours measures knowledge of specific rights rather than awareness of the GDPR and distinguishes uncertainty from mistaken belief (see below).
Not knowing one's data rights took two forms.

Most respondents with poor knowledge were uncertain (CLASS-1 and CLASS-2, about a third of each sample), while about a tenth (CLASS-3) answered that rights were not in force, which may reflect wrong information or doubt that rights work in practice, or simply a guess.
In practice, information campaigns may help the uncertain group, while the misinformed group may also need examples of rights being enforced.

Finally, sociodemographic characteristics explained little of any measure or of class membership, and the classes were only weakly related to trust, risk-taking or life satisfaction, so they reflect orientations towards privacy rather than general traits.

Group differences in knowledge were real but small next to the deficit that all groups shared, suggesting that the lack of a link between sensitivity and rights knowledge is not specific to particular groups and may reflect how people encounter their data in everyday services.

European data protection law and policy rely on individuals using their rights to take control of their data (European Commission, 2019b), assuming that people who care about their data and privacy will find out what they can do about it.
Our results do not support this assumption: knowledge of rights was limited and unequally distributed, and it was not related to sensitivity, which was widespread and rising.
Raising concern, whether through public cases or campaigns, is therefore unlikely by itself to make people better able to use their rights.
This does not mean giving up the individual's role, which becomes more necessary as more decisions are based on data (see Introduction).
But a deficit that is shared across the population and stable over time is unlikely to be closed by individual effort or information campaigns alone.
Knowledge of rights needs to be built into the places where people view or use their personal data, such as e-government portals, and it needs to reach older and non-Estonian residents in particular.

In Estonia, services such as the Data Tracker (Solvak and Lauringson, 2024) could tell people which right they are using when they view their data, and what else they can do: correct the data, restrict its processing or object to conclusions drawn from it.
text.formatted: In Estonia, services such as the Data Tracker <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Solvak and Lauringson, 2024)</ref> could tell people which right they are using when they view their data, and what else they can do: correct the data, restrict its processing or object to conclusions drawn from it.

text.text: Identifying and understanding one's own data are the first steps towards acting on it (Pangrazio and Selwyn, 2019), and such services could make these steps part of ordinary use.

Future research could test whether contact with or knowledge of one's own data builds knowledge of rights and links it to concern; and whether knowing a right leads to using it, by linking surveys to records of rights exercised.
The surveys used a quota-based online panel rather than a probability sample, and all analyses are unweighted.
Change over time rests on two independent samples, so we cannot distinguish a trend from a fluctuation or attribute the changes to any particular cause.
Wave 3 also differed in composition and in the wording of the income question; all differences held when composition was controlled (Appendix D1), but the adjustment for income is imperfect.
All measures are self-reports.
Privacy sensitivity was measured with single four-point items, and importance was rated close to the top of the scale, leaving little room for increase.
Because all six rights listed are in force, a general tendency to answer "in force" would raise knowledge scores; future surveys could include rights that do not exist.
The translation of the rights items from Estonian to Russian may have affected answers, in particular the ethnic difference in knowledge.
Knowing a right is not the same as using it, and the surveys did not observe privacy behaviour or the exercise of rights.
The order of question blocks differed in Wave 3, but a general shift towards agreeing is unlikely, because the share of "in force" answers did not rise.
Because many tests were run without correction for multiple comparisons, isolated small effects should be read with caution.
Comparisons of classes across waves are descriptive, as classes were matched by inspection, and CLASS-1 in Wave 1 differed most from its later counterparts.
The independence of sensitivity and knowledge was not tested within subgroups.
Finally, whether the patterns hold in societies less digitalised than Estonia remains open.
In a highly digitalised society, caring about privacy and personal data and knowing one's data protection rights turned out to be separate.
Across three waves over two and a half years, privacy and data sensitivity were high and rose, while knowledge of rights remained low and unrelated to them.

Where such knowledge is low and unequal, rights place little practical constraint on data processing: the rights-based model leaves control with those who hold the data and protects mainly those who already know how to claim their rights.

Building this knowledge into the services where people use their data is therefore a responsibility of the institutions that provide them, and a condition for people to take part in decisions about their data.
